Back exercise

Barbell Row

The bent-over barbell row is the main horizontal pull for building back thickness. It balances out pressing work and strengthens the hip hinge you use in deadlifts.

By Khushi Gupta · Reviewed October 2026

Primary
Back
Also works
Lats, Rear delts, Biceps, Lower back
Equipment
Barbell, plates
Level
Intermediate

How to do it

  1. Stand with feet hip width, the bar over your mid-foot, and grip it slightly wider than shoulder width with palms facing you or down.
  2. Deadlift the bar to standing, then hinge forward by pushing your hips back with a soft knee bend.
  3. Lower your torso to about 30 to 45 degrees above horizontal. Keep your back flat and let the bar hang at arm's length below your shoulders.
  4. Brace your abs and keep your neck in line with your spine.
  5. Pull the bar toward your lower ribs or upper stomach, driving your elbows back and squeezing your shoulder blades together.
  6. Pause briefly when the bar touches your torso.
  7. Lower the bar under control until your arms are straight, keeping your torso angle fixed.

Coaching cues

  • Elbows to your back pockets
  • Torso stays still
  • Squeeze the shoulder blades at the top
  • Flat back, braced core
Advertisements

Common mistakes and fixes

Standing up more with every rep

Pick a load you can row with a fixed torso angle. If you need to heave, it is too heavy.

Rounding the lower back

Brace before each set, keep your chest up, and reduce the weight. Strengthen the hinge with Romanian deadlifts.

Pulling with the arms only

Think about driving the elbows back rather than curling the bar. Your hands are just hooks.

Shrugging the shoulders toward the ears

Keep the shoulders down and pull back and slightly down, toward the hips.

Sets and reps

GoalPrescription
Strength3-5 sets of 5-8 reps, 2-3 minutes rest
Hypertrophy3-4 sets of 8-12 reps, 90-120 seconds rest
Beginner3 sets of 8 reps with a weight you control fully

Pick a starting weight with the one rep max calculator, and load the bar with the plate calculator.

Variations

  • Pendlay row Each rep starts from the floor with a flat torso, building explosive pulling power.
  • Chest supported row Lying face down on an incline bench removes lower back fatigue.
  • One-arm dumbbell row Lets you pull through a longer range and fix imbalances.
  • Seated cable row Constant tension and an easy way to learn the pull.

Muscles worked

Rowing pulls your arms back toward your torso, which works the lats, rhomboids, middle trapezius and rear delts. Your biceps and forearms assist the elbow bend.

Holding the bent-over position also makes your spinal erectors, glutes and hamstrings work hard isometrically, which is why rows feel taxing on the lower back.

Benefits

A strong row builds a thick upper back that supports heavy squats and deadlifts and gives the bench press a stable base. It also offsets the rounded shoulder posture that comes from lots of pressing and desk work.

Most balanced programmes include roughly as much rowing as pressing. The upper lower split pairs them on every upper day.

Safety and who should modify it

If your lower back gets tired before your upper back, switch to a chest supported or one-arm dumbbell row. You keep the benefit for the back muscles without loading the spine.

Anyone with a history of disc problems should start with supported rows and only add the bent-over version once a neutral hinge feels comfortable under load.

Frequently asked questions

Overhand or underhand grip?

Overhand slightly favours the upper back and rear delts; underhand brings in more biceps and lats and lets many people lift a little more. Both are good choices.

Where should the bar touch?

Around the bottom of your rib cage or upper stomach. Pulling higher toward the chest shifts work to the upper back and rear delts.

Is the barbell row better than a cable row?

Not better, different. The barbell row allows heavier loads and trains the hinge; cable rows are easier to recover from and to do with strict form.
